name: Priya Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Priya, 58, and lead developers at a tech company that records grain deliveries for storage depots. I have a master’s degree and know the weighbridge and moisture records better than most people on the team. I compare the driver’s paper ticket with the stored weight, then review any code that changes a payment. I have never used AI tools; the farmer needs a person who can explain each number.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Dev repairs garden equipment and gets paid by the job; our children are grown. My lead pay is low for the work, his repair bookings vary, and we still have a mortgage. We have about three weeks of expenses saved and few other developer jobs nearby. Retirement is near enough to discuss, but we have no verified income figure that covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the depot AI Plateau leaves someone needing to read the scale ticket before paying a farmer. A clean dashboard cannot replace a missing load of grain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still worry about Dev’s variable repair work and three weeks saved. My lead job holds, but a slow workshop month and a mortgage bill can collide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking digital weights against paper weighbridge tickets with the depot clerk. I’d put 30 aside on paydays only after mortgage and groceries. In the first year I’d keep a second signature on corrected grain payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the ordinary cash gap, not about AI here. I know the system well, but knowing it does not refill the savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which scale ticket required a correction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A truck’s ticket had a handwritten correction after the scale printer jammed. The clerk showed me the original weight before I changed the payment record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you replace the gate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev and I would repair our old gate rather than replace it. We would keep cash for the mortgage instead of spending on a tidy entrance.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking grain tickets.
I would keep **second signatures** on corrected farmer payments.
think: I worry Dev’s **repair bookings** may fall in an ordinary month.
Our **three-week reserve** leaves little room around the mortgage.
do: **Compare** digital weights with paper tickets and clerk review.
**Require** second signatures on corrected payments and repair the old gate rather than replace it.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills despite secure lead work.
S0.quote: A clean dashboard cannot replace a missing load of grain.
fieldNote: Her **weighbridge knowledge** and clerk checks hold the payment trail together without AI.
The **three-week reserve** and Dev’s variable repair bookings make baseline money pressure real.

steps.text: Keep checking grain payments against paper weighbridge tickets with clerk sign-off
Save 30 only after mortgage and groceries
Repair old gate rather than replace it; retain cash for mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write and check grain-payment code before robots handle sacks and scales. I would demand a clerk’s signature when an automated change lowers a farmer’s payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company may keep me to supervise more code with fewer colleagues. My own hours look steady this year, but one lost contract could change that quickly with no savings cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d put six disputed weight tickets in a folder and show management how each was settled by a clerk. I’d keep leading paid reviews while our depot contract holds. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d search real depot-software vacancies only with written pay that, alongside Dev’s usual repair fees, covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our three-week reserve and the pressure on the team, though my own pay holds for now. I would speak up before a clerk becomes a decorative signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which disputed ticket would you show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One load was recorded dry although rain had soaked it during unloading. I would bring both the paper moisture reading and the driver’s note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Dev add repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would take repair jobs that customers actually book. We would not budget for every person who asks for a price.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach payment code before warehouse robots.
I would insist on **clerk sign-off** for lower farmer payments.
think: I expect my **lead hours** to hold for now.
I worry **one lost depot contract** could change our pay quickly.
do: **Show** six clerk-settled weight disputes to management.
**Keep** paid code reviews while depot contract holds.
**Search** real depot-software posts if hours fall and written pay covers mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline cash and team cuts, despite current lead income.
S1.quote: I would speak up before a clerk becomes a decorative signature.
fieldNote: She uses **six paper disputes** to hold management to accountable payment checks.
Her **three-week reserve** and variable repairs keep her anxious even while her lead hours hold for now.

steps.text: Keep paid grain-code reviews and show six clerk-settled weight disputes
Search real depot-software posts if hours fall only with mortgage-covering pay alongside usual repair fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the depot AGI by 2028 could do grain-payment code in 2028, with hands-on warehouse robots around 2031. Dev’s repair quotes may change before a robot handles a mower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my lead post could go despite my experience. Three weeks saved would not carry the mortgage through a long search, and local code jobs may vanish together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request written layoff terms and call the mortgage lender early if my wage ends. We would cancel our planned family visit before paying train fares and keep cash for housing. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible help; I would not treat our children’s wages as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and awake at night about losing my wage. A low-paid lead title does not buy extra months of food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the visit is delayed, not ask them to pay for our tickets. They have bills where they live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Dev’s shop cover the bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would continue paid repairs while customers bring equipment. A quoted job is not income until somebody accepts and pays for it.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach grain code before 2031 warehouse robots.
I would say **repair quoting** changes before hands-on work.
think: I expect my **lead post** could go.
I cannot rely on **local software jobs** after full thinking AI.
do: **Request** written terms and contact lender early if wage ends.
**Cancel** family visit before fares and hold mortgage cash.
**Apply** to real paid openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless about losing lead pay.
S2.quote: A low-paid lead title does not buy extra months of food.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 code loss**, three years before physical warehouse robots arrive.
Her **thin cash buffer** drives travel cancellation, early lender contact and conditional help.

steps.text: Cancel planned family visit before paying train fares
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches grain code in 2031 and warehouse robots around 2034. Five years lets me ask whether a depot actually pays people to inspect grain on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect code work to shrink. I can read the moisture record, but I have never been the person taking the sample, and a physical role may shrink when robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the depot clerk for permission to accompany an inspector on two Saturdays using depot equipment and a supervisor. I’d do it only if it costs no training fee, I lose no paid developer hours, and Dev and I can keep our usual family time. In the first year after 2031, if my coding ends, I’d apply only to a real paid grain-inspection vacancy still hiring people despite 2034 robots, with a written wage that covers mortgage and groceries alongside Dev’s usual accepted repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my code wage, with time to check a real place. An unpaid certificate would be another bill, not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from the inspector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wet sample can look dry on a screen if the bag was labelled for another load. I would need supervised practice taking and sealing a sample.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What income would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would keep the garden-equipment jobs customers actually pay for. We would not use repair quotes or our children’s incomes to make an inspector wage look adequate.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 warehouse robots.
I would check **paid grain-inspection work** before changing fields.
think: I expect **grain-code work** could shrink when full thinking AI arrives in 2031.
I know **field inspection** might also change when warehouse robots arrive around 2034.
do: **Shadow** grain inspector on two Saturdays only with depot permission, equipment, supervision, no training fee or lost paid hours.
**Keep** agreed family Saturdays while testing the field role.
**Apply** after 2031 coding loss only to paid posts still hiring people, with wages covering mortgage and groceries alongside Dev’s accepted repairs.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with time to test field work.
S3.quote: An unpaid certificate would be another bill, not a job.
fieldNote: Her **two-Saturday field test** is free, supervised, approved and does not cost paid work or family time.
A **grain-inspection move** requires real hiring after 2031 and a wage sufficient with accepted repair income.

steps.text: Shadow two Saturdays only with depot approval, supplied equipment, supervision, no fee or lost paid hours
Keep agreed family Saturdays during field shadowing
If coding ends after 2031, apply to real posts covering mortgage and groceries with accepted repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 reaches grain code in 2036; hands-on warehouse robots come around 2039. A decade would let us check paid apprenticeships and actual retirement figures before we claim we can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry our firm could squeeze even lead hours before 2036. Three weeks saved is too little to retire on, and no one has shown us a reliable pension amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the paper-ticket checks while paid and save 30 after mortgage and groceries. Dev and I would request written retirement statements and a mortgage balance each year. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if verified income and savings cover housing and ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the thin buffer even with ten years. More time helps only if the paid weeks keep arriving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for our own retirement statements, not work from a neighbour’s age. We have no reason to count the children’s wages as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave the clerk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave the clerk a clear list of how each corrected weight was approved. A handwritten ticket still has a driver behind it.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 warehouse robots.
I would check **paid apprenticeships** and verified retirement resources.
think: I worry **lead hours** could shrink before the full 2036 code change arrives.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot fund retirement while our mortgage remains unpaid.
do: **Keep** paper-ticket checks and save 30 only after essentials.
**Request** annual retirement statements and mortgage balances with Dev.
**Seek** real paid work if coding ends after 2036; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Anxious** about existing thin savings despite ten years.
S4.quote: A handwritten ticket still has a driver behind it.
fieldNote: She keeps **paper evidence** and conditional savings while working toward verified retirement figures.
The **retirement gate** uses written household resources, not assumed pensions or children’s wages.

steps.text: Keep checking grain payments against paper tickets while paid
Save 30 only after mortgage and groceries
Seek real paid openings if code ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our savings would be gone before a local job search had much chance. Written terms, a real paid opening and eligible help would matter. A verified inspection apprenticeship would be useful only if it paid enough to keep the mortgage current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the depot clerk to show the driver’s original ticket before changing a grain payment. A clean screen does not weigh a truck.

headlineQuote: A clean screen does not weigh a truck.
portrait: Priya is a **58-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree, lower pay and three weeks saved.
She never uses **AI tools**, relying on weighbridge tickets, clerks and second signatures.
Her partner’s **repair fees** vary; few local developer jobs and a mortgage keep her anxious.
She explores **supervised grain inspection** only without fees or lost pay and with a real adequate vacancy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could empty their savings before local paid work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, a real paid opening and eligible help would matter; any apprenticeship needs mortgage-covering pay.
